procedural_history.impugned_order: Order made by the President on the 17th April, 1953, under Note 1 to article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution praying that the President's order be quashed on the ground that it was illegal and void because it was made without affording him any opportunity.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court because he believed that article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations could not be supported as a valid rule under subsections (2), (3) or (4) of section 96B and can have no application to the appellant who was appointed by the Secretary of State in Council and consequently the order of the President made m accordance with Note l to that article is illegal and void.

directions: In the circumstances of this. case we make no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether Note 1 to Article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations, which provides for compulsory retirement, is applicable to the appellant who was appointed by the Secretary of State in Council.

facts: The appellant was appointed by the Secretary of State in Council in 1923.
The government sought to compulsorily retire the appellant under Note 1 to Article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations.

The appellant argued that this rule was not applicable to him because it was created in 1920, after the Government of India Act, 1919, was passed, and was not made by the Secretary of State in Council.
law: Section 96B(4) of the Government of India Act, 1919, gave statutory force to all civil service rules that were in operation at the time the Act was passed (December 23, 1919).

On November 15, 1919, the Government of India, with the approval of the Secretary of State, announced new rules on retiring pensions via Resolution No. 1085-E.A. This included a rule (new rule 4) allowing for the compulsory retirement of an officer after 25 years of service.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument by tracing the origin of the compulsory retirement rule.
The Court found that the rule allowing compulsory retirement was first announced in a resolution on November 15, 1919.
Because this resolution was published and in force before the Government of India Act, 1919, was passed, the rule gained statutory force under Section 96B(4) of that Act.

The Court determined that the subsequent incorporation of this rule into the Civil Service Regulations in 1920 as Article 465-A and Note 1 was not the creation of a new rule. Instead, it was done to clarify the scope of the existing 1919 rule and place it in the regulations for easy reference.

To support this, the Court analyzed the language of Note 1, which states the government "retains" the right to compulsorily retire an officer. The Court reasoned that one can only "retain" a right that one already possesses. This pre-existing right was the one established by the November 1919 resolution.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the government's right to compulsorily retire the appellant was derived from a rule that was validated and confirmed by the Government of India Act, 1919. Therefore, Note 1 to Article 465-A, which merely referenced this pre-existing right, was applicable to the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the rule for compulsory retirement (Note 1 to Article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations) became void upon the commencement of the Constitution for being repugnant to Article 311, on the ground that compulsory retirement amounts to removal from service without an opportunity to show cause.

facts: The appellant argued that the rule allowing for compulsory retirement (Note 1 to Article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations) was unconstitutional.
The basis of the argument was that compulsory retirement is the same as 'removal' from service.
Article 311 of the Constitution requires that a person being 'removed' from service must be given an opportunity to show cause.
The compulsory retirement rule did not provide for such an opportunity.
law: The Supreme Court established that while 'removal' is a type of termination of service, not every termination of service amounts to 'removal' as understood in Article 311.
The Court identified two key characteristics of 'removal' or 'dismissal':
1. It implies that the officer is blameworthy, deficient, or guilty of misconduct. It involves leveling a charge or imputation against the officer and carries a stigma.
2. It is a form of punishment that results in the loss of benefits already earned by the officer, such as their pension.
application: The Court analyzed compulsory retirement against the two characteristics of 'removal'.

First, it found that compulsory retirement does not involve any 'stigma or implication of misbehaviour or incapacity'. It is not based on a specific charge or imputation against the officer but on the grounds of completing 25 years of service and the public interest in dispensing with their further services.

Second, the Court determined that compulsory retirement is not a punishment because the officer does not lose any earned benefits. An officer who is compulsorily retired is still entitled to the full pension and other benefits they have accrued, unlike an officer who is removed or dismissed.
Since compulsory retirement lacks the essential elements of 'removal' (i.e., stigma and punitive loss of benefits), the Court concluded that the two are distinct actions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that compulsory retirement does not amount to 'removal' within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution. Because it is not a 'removal', the constitutional requirement of providing an opportunity to show cause does not apply. Therefore, the rule for compulsory retirement (Note 1 to Article 465-A) was not repugnant to the Constitution and was not void.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Note 1 to Article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations, which provides for compulsory retirement, is applicable to the appellant who was appointed by the Secretary of State in Council.
appellant_arguments: Note 1 to Article 465-A cannot be supported as a valid rule under sub-sections (2), (3), or (4) of section 96B of the Government of India Act, 1919.
Consequently, the rule has no application to the appellant, who was appointed by the Secretary of State in Council, making the President's order illegal and void.
respondent_arguments: The rule for compulsory retirement originated from Resolution No. 1085-E.A. of 1919, which was announced with the approval of the Secretary of State for India.
By virtue of sub-section (4) of section 96B of the Government of India Act, 1919, this rule became binding on the appellant, even though he was employed by the Secretary of State for India.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the rule for compulsory retirement (Note 1 to Article 465-A of the Civil Service Regulations) became void upon the commencement of the Constitution for being repugnant to Article 311, on the ground that compulsory retirement amounts to removal from service without an opportunity to show cause.
appellant_arguments: Compulsory retirement is nothing but a 'removal from service' within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution.
Since Note 1 to Article 465-A allows for compulsory retirement without giving the officer an opportunity to show cause, it is repugnant to the provisions of Article 311.
Therefore, the rule became void upon the commencement of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: Compulsory retirement is not the same as 'removal from service' as contemplated by Article 311. (Inferred from the court's rejection of the appellant's 'plausible and attractive' argument and its reliance on precedent).

cases.principle: That removal was within section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which implies that removal is comprised within dismissal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A compulsory retirement of an officer, sanctioned by a valid service rule, does not constitute a "removal" from service within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution, and therefore does not attract the procedural safeguards of that article.
obiter: Under the Constitution, removal and dismissal stand on the same footing, with the only distinction being that dismissal disqualifies from future employment while removal does not; in this sense, removal is a species of dismissal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A compulsory retirement does not amount to dismissal or removal within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution and therefore does not attract its procedural safeguards. The court established a two-part test to distinguish them: unlike dismissal or removal, compulsory retirement carries no stigma or implication of misbehaviour, and it is not a punishment because the officer does not lose any earned benefits, such as pension. Therefore, an order of compulsory retirement cannot be challenged on the ground that the officer was not afforded a full opportunity to show cause.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the termination of service carries a stigma or implication of misbehaviour or incapacity.
Whether the termination of service is a punishment that involves the loss of benefits already earned by the officer, such as pension.
why_appellant_lost: The court found that the right to compulsorily retire the appellant was not derived from Note 1 to Article 465-A itself, but from a pre-existing rule announced by Resolution No. 1085-E.A. on November 15, 1919. This rule was in operation at the time of the Government of India Act, 1919, and by virtue of its section 96B(4), it became binding on the appellant.

The appellant's argument that compulsory retirement is equivalent to 'removal from service' under Article 311 was rejected. The court held that compulsory retirement has no stigma or implication of misbehaviour or incapacity, which is a principal test for determining if a termination is a dismissal or removal.

The court determined that compulsory retirement is not a punishment. Unlike an officer who is dismissed or removed and loses their earned pension, an officer who is compulsorily retired is entitled to the pension and other benefits they have actually earned, with no diminution of accrued benefits.
Because compulsory retirement is neither a dismissal nor a removal, the provisions of Article 311, which require an opportunity for the officer to show cause against the action, are not applicable.
why_respondent_won: The government's right to compulsorily retire the appellant was traced back to Resolution No. 1085-E.A. of 1919, which had the approval of the Secretary of State for India and became binding on the appellant via section 96B(4) of the Government of India Act, 1919.

The court accepted that the language of Note 1 to Article 465-A, specifically the word 'retains', indicates that the government was not conferring a new right but was acknowledging a pre-existing one derived from the 1919 Resolution.

The court established that compulsory retirement is distinct from dismissal or removal because it does not meet the two key tests: it carries no stigma and it is not a punishment involving the loss of earned benefits.
As compulsory retirement falls outside the definition of dismissal or removal, the government was not required to comply with the procedural requirements of Article 311 of the Constitution.
policy_considerations: The right to compulsorily retire an officer is to be exercised when it is in the public interest to dispense with the further services of that officer.

The power of compulsory retirement may be used when an authority cannot substantiate misconduct which may be the real cause for the action, as an imputation or charge is not a necessary condition for its exercise.

An inquiry preceding a compulsory retirement may be conducted simply to help the Government make up its mind as to whether it is in the public interest to dispense with an officer's services, rather than as a formal disciplinary proceeding.
